These are between-worlds that disappear, one after another, to leave the path free for this dissatisfied painter, refusing at once the black square on a black ground and the white square on a white ground, for it is in the interposition of the two that his possibles, his new visions, begin to be born. That day in Rio resembled, as if by chance, the whiteness and the darkness of your words recounting to me the fate of your grandfather, stricken by the gaze of the Medusa. The white cane thus becomes the invisible canvas, the painting to be created, while your grandfather’s wounded body serves as shadow to the gaze that wishes to install itself in a concrete pictorial utopia. The white cane is the brush over the darkness, like the staff of the hero of Moby Dick, a whale bone. I have often understood that modern painting always stands in need of a minimalist blindness, whether symbolized by the memory of a next of kin, in order to engage upon the difficult path of the invisible, to lean upon the white cane of the one who would like to learn to look with the third eye.
